title: Reading an IR source
description: Carry the published file reader into a new language workshop.
why: A translator begins by reading its source reliably. We shall use the file reader already constructed in ASM86, with an IR filename and a diagnostic display.
explain:
Begin with the saved AS07.ASM program from the ASM86 collection. Its GETNAME, OPENFILE, NEXTBYTE, READLINE, and CLOSEFILE routines provide the complete input path. The source extension is .IR; the DOS output strings still end in a dollar sign, and file extensions end in a zero byte.

READLINE returns AX=1 with uppercase text at 2200H, or AX=0 at end of file. ZTEXT walks a zero-terminated line from SI and changes AX, DX, and SI. The driver resets SI for each line and displays a separate CR/LF. LINENO counts physical lines, including comments and blank lines.

This is a text diagnostic. It performs no language translation and creates no assembly output. The inherited reader admits 120 physical characters per line and rejects an overrun before writing outside its buffer. It retains the full-segment stack check and the DOS failure status.

title: Seeing the tokens
description: Separate words and punctuation without losing the line cursor.
why: A physical line is not yet an instruction. The scanner can show exactly which tokens a parser receives.
explain:
SCAN is the published ASM86 scanner. SI is its source cursor; the result is a zero-terminated token at 2300H and a word length in TOKLEN. AX and DI are scratch registers. Spaces are skipped, comma and brackets are individual tokens, and semicolon ends the statement.

The driver saves SI while ZTEXT displays the token, then restores it before calling SCAN again. The bracket characters on the display are diagnostic decoration, not source syntax. An empty token ends the current statement.

The token bound is sixteen characters plus its zero terminator. This bound is independent of the physical-line bound. No quoted-string rule is added. A long unbroken word is rejected even when the entire physical line fits.

title: Buffering assembly text
description: Keep a complete text result before creating its output file.
why: We shall collect text in memory, then write one .ASM file only after the input has been accepted.
explain:
OUTPTR begins at 6000H. EMITCHAR takes one character in AL and advances that pointer, preserving AX and BX. It checks the E000H upper bound before a store. OUTTEXT walks a zero-terminated string from SI and sends each character through EMITCHAR; SI, AL, and flags are scratch.

WRITEOUT changes the saved extension to .ASM, uses DOS function 3CH to create or truncate the output, and writes the collected count with function 40H. Carry and the returned byte count are checked. CLOSEFILE must succeed before the OK report. A read or syntax failure leaves an older output untouched; a write or close failure can leave a partial file.

The success count is a count of assembly-text bytes, including CR/LF, not a machine-code image size. At this checkpoint the source lines are simply copied in normalized form. The test is data for inspection, not an executable program.

title: Inspecting an instruction record
description: Search fixed records and display the target-size field.
why: Before using an instruction record to select target text, we can inspect the result of its lookup directly.
explain:
LOOK is the published ASM86 table search. BX supplies the table address, CX its count, and AX a record stride of fourteen bytes. It returns a record in BX or zero and preserves the source cursor SI. The record begins with a zero-padded name.

After the eight name bytes, each record holds an argument class, expression effect, target-byte count, one padding byte, and a word pointer to its text pattern. The driver advances to the target-byte field, clears AH, and passes the value to NUMBER. FINISH rejects an unwanted operand before anything is reported.

The text-output routines from the preceding checkpoint remain in the source. This diagnostic does not call them or create an assembly file. Keeping the tested routines in place avoids entering them again merely to inspect a table lookup. The display distinguishes NOP and HALT and a missing name is an explicit syntax error.

title: Selecting a translation pattern
description: A small instruction table selects fixed assembly text.
why: Repeated target sequences belong in a table. We shall recognize NOP and HALT and emit their fixed assembly patterns.
explain:
LOOK is the published fixed-record search. BX is the table base, CX the record count, and AX the stride. It returns a record in BX or zero, preserving the source cursor SI. Each IR record reserves eight bytes for its zero-padded name, then argument class, stack effect, target byte count, one padding byte, and a word template pointer. The stride is fourteen.

STATEMENT retains these fields before another routine can change the lookup registers. FINISH rejects an extra token. EXPAND walks the selected zero-terminated assembly pattern from SI; the patterns currently contain only literal characters. Templates are text data, not preassembled instruction bytes.

HALT emits a zero-status DOS termination. LAST records a terminal instruction so the normal end-of-source exit need not be repeated. When the last statement can fall through, FINISHOUTPUT appends HALT. Its target is the same documented ASM86 instruction vocabulary.

title: Substituting a name
description: Save one checked name and insert it behind a safe prefix.
why: A fixed text pattern cannot name a program location. We shall give a template a checked name to insert.
explain:
NAMEARG scans and validates a name, then copies it to 2500H while preserving the source cursor. A name begins with a letter or underscore and continues with letters, digits, or underscores. Its maximum is fourteen characters, leaving room for U_ within ASM86's name bound.

An @ in a template substitutes the saved name. EXPAND saves SI while OUTTEXT reads the saved name, then restores SI to resume the template. LABEL emits U_name and a colon on a standalone assembly line. An IR name such as AX is harmless because U_AX is not a register.

This checkpoint has no enforced MAIN entry point or declaration area. A label emits no bytes; execution still starts at the first emitted instruction. The test places a label before NOP and HALT, and NAMEARG rejects a name beginning with a digit.

title: Naming the entry point
description: Prefix names and require MAIN before executable statements.
why: A source needs an entry point and a namespace which cannot collide with registers or translator labels.
explain:
NAMEARG scans and validates a name, then copies it to 2500H while preserving the line cursor. Names begin with a letter or underscore and contain letters, digits, or underscores. Their limit is fourteen characters: the emitted U_ prefix must still fit ASM86's sixteen-character label limit. Register spellings can be IR names because the prefix keeps them distinct.

The @ character in a template inserts that saved name. EXPAND saves SI while OUTTEXT walks the substitution, then resumes the template. LABEL emits a standalone U_name definition. CONTEXT requires the first executable label to be MAIN; ordinary executable statements require that code context.

The header clears direction, checks the full-segment entry stack, and jumps over the declaration area to U_MAIN. A smaller entry stack returns status seven. I_ENTRY belongs to the translator's namespace. The final source must contain MAIN; missing names and duplicate definitions in emitted assembly remain ASM86 diagnostics.

title: Loading an unsigned word
description: Validate numeric spelling before inserting it in a MOV.
why: The accumulator needs a value. LIT supplies an unsigned word, and EXIT makes its low byte observable as a DOS status.
explain:
AX is the IR accumulator. LIT emits MOV AX,value. NUMARG uses the published unsigned decimal and hexadecimal reader, saves the numeric result in NUMV, and copies its checked spelling to 2520H. The # template marker inserts that spelling. VALUE preserves SI; AX, BX, CX, DX, DI, BP, and flags are scratch.

Numbers range from zero through 65535. Hexadecimal ends in H and begins with a decimal digit, as in 0FFH. Signs, expressions, and character literals are excluded so the translator can validate one token without evaluating a language expression.

EXIT emits a DOS termination using the low byte of AX. HALT always returns zero. EXIT is therefore suitable for testing a computed zero result; a nonzero low byte deliberately produces the checker's FAIL report. Arithmetic words and DOS status bytes have different widths.

title: Declaring a word
description: Put initialized word storage before the entry label.
why: WORD gives a value a named place in memory, separate from the accumulator.
explain:
WORD takes a name and an unsigned initializer. ARGUMENTS retains the name before scanning its value, since both use the same token buffer. Its template emits U_name followed by DW value. ASM86 writes the initializer low byte first.

Declarations must precede LABEL MAIN. The header jumps over them, so no declaration byte is executed at program entry. CONTEXT accepts declaration classes only while CODE is zero, and the MAIN label changes CODE to one.

A declaration emits storage in the program's single segment. A name has one common namespace for storage and code; the translator checks spelling while ASM86 resolves references and rejects duplicate definitions. A successful translation is not permission to run a file whose assembly failed.

title: Loading and storing a word
description: Move between AX and a named word without changing its address.
why: A declaration becomes useful when the program can read it and replace its value.
explain:
LD name emits MOV AX,[U_name]. ST name emits MOV [U_name],AX and retains the accumulator. Both transfer a word at DS:offset; a word occupies two consecutive bytes. The name operand is checked by NAMEARG and resolved by ASM86.

These templates use direct memory operands, so BX is not required to hold the address. They do not imply that the translator tracks a declaration's type. The programmer must pair a word access with storage large enough for a word.

The test stores zero into a word initialized to seven, then loads it after replacing AX with 99. EXIT must receive zero. This distinguishes a working load from an unchanged accumulator and a working store from the original initializer.

title: Byte storage
description: Check byte initializers and clear the high half of a byte load.
why: Text and file input are bytes. BYTE, LDB, and STB make that width explicit without changing the word accumulator.
explain:
BYTE declares one initialized byte and refuses an initializer above 255. The common number reader still returns a word; the declaration handler applies the narrower range. STB writes AL and retains AX. LDB loads AL and then clears AH, returning a value from zero through 255.

The same U_ namespace is used for byte and word storage. Width belongs to the operation, not a type inferred from the name. A word access to the last byte of a buffer can reach adjacent storage; the translator cannot protect such a runtime access.

The test replaces the initialized byte with zero, disturbs AX, and loads the byte again. Inspect the emitted MOV AH,0 as well as the zero exit status: it is the operation which makes a byte load an unsigned word result.

title: A bounded expression stack
description: Save AX and retrieve it with an explicit stack effect.
why: One accumulator cannot retain both sides of an expression. PUSH saves its word; POP restores the latest saved word.
explain:
The expression stack uses native PUSH AX and POP AX. DEPTH is a translation-time count, initially zero. FLOW checks each table effect before emitting it: PUSH adds one, POP requires a saved word and removes one, and a control boundary requires an empty expression stack. BALANCED performs that common boundary check.

The bound is thirty-two saved words. It limits expression bookkeeping and temporary stack demand without pretending to limit the CPU's stack. Native call return addresses also use SS:SP, so an expression may not cross a label, branch, procedure call, return, or termination. Each basic block starts and ends with an empty expression stack.

This simple rule avoids a control-flow analysis of different stack depths arriving at one label. It permits straight expressions within a block and makes an unmatched POP a translation error. AX and arithmetic flags are scratch state in FLOW; its counters belong to the translator, not the emitted program.

title: Adding and subtracting
description: Combine a saved left operand with the accumulator right operand.
why: An arithmetic operation can consume the saved left operand and leave its result in AX.
explain:
ADD pops the left word into BX and adds it to AX. SUB must retain operand order: it pops BX, subtracts AX from BX, and copies BX to AX. Thus LIT 7, PUSH, LIT 3, SUB computes seven minus three.

Both operations require one saved word and reduce DEPTH by one. Their arithmetic wraps modulo 65536; there is no overflow exception or signed-literal syntax. The same word bits can be interpreted as unsigned or signed when an operation explicitly says which comparison to make.

BX and arithmetic flags are scratch registers for these emitted operations. AX is the result. The test combines subtraction and addition and finally subtracts the known result, so CHECK can report a visible PASS for a computed zero.

title: Word-sized bit operations
description: AND, OR, and XOR use the same operand discipline.
why: Bit masks and packed fields need logical operations on the complete word.
explain:
Each pattern pops the saved word into BX and applies the selected word operation to AX and BX. AND retains bits set in both, OR retains bits set in either, and XOR retains bits which differ. AX receives the word result; BX and flags are scratch.

The table supplies the same consume-one stack effect as ADD. There is no separate parser for each mnemonic. A missing left operand is still a stack error, not a zero value silently supplied by the translator.

The test forms (15 AND 10) XOR 3 OR 1, which is nine, then subtracts nine. Unsigned decimal spelling is used for the masks; equivalent hexadecimal spelling is accepted by the existing numeric reader.

title: Addresses as word values
description: Form an address and fetch through the accumulator.
why: A loop needs to advance a pointer instead of naming every byte separately. ADDR produces an offset as an ordinary word.
explain:
ADDR name emits MOV AX,U_name. FETCH copies that offset to BX and reads a word through [BX]. FETCHB reads one byte and clears AH. Both replace the address in AX with the fetched value; BX and flags are scratch.

All addresses are offsets in DS, which remains the DOS program segment. No segment value or far pointer is introduced. A pointer can be advanced with the existing word arithmetic. The programmer must keep it within allocated storage and allow two bytes for a word fetch.

The test fetches a declared word and a byte through their addresses, adds the two zero values, and returns zero. The emitted target uses exactly the BX-based memory form already accepted by ASM86.

title: Writing through an address
description: Consume a saved pointer and retain the value being stored.
why: A buffer writer needs a pointer and a value at the same time. The expression stack can retain the pointer while AX receives the value.
explain:
PUT pops the address into BX and writes AX through [BX]. PUTB writes AL instead. AX retains the stored word in either case, while the expression stack loses the saved pointer. The width of the operation determines how many bytes are written.

The order is address, PUSH, value, PUT. It differs from an arithmetic left operand only in the meaning of the saved word. FLOW applies the same consume-one check, so a missing address cannot accidentally pop a native return address.

These operations perform no runtime bounds check. The test uses declared storage, replaces nonzero initializers with zero through pointers, then reads the named locations and adds their values before EXIT.

title: Reserving a byte buffer
description: Emit bounded, zero-filled storage without a string syntax.
why: BUFFER names a run of consecutive bytes which pointer operations can traverse.
explain:
BUFFER takes a name and a count from one through 256. NUMV retains that count. ZEROBUFFER first expands the name definition, then emits DB rows of at most sixteen zero values. CX counts bytes still required and BP counts the current row. OUTTEXT and EMITCHAR preserve those counters.

Grouping the zeroes keeps each assembly line short and avoids spending one source line per byte. The final row may be partial. Each row ends with CR/LF, and no extra alignment byte is inserted.

The count is deliberately bounded so a declaration remains easy to inspect. Larger working areas can be addressed explicitly within the allocated segment, but that requires a memory plan; BUFFER itself reserves bytes in the emitted image. The test crosses a row boundary and fetches its initial zero byte.

title: Counting the target image
description: Check machine-byte demand separately from assembly-text length.
why: The assembly text and the program it describes have different sizes. Both need their own bounds.
explain:
Each instruction record carries its emitted machine-byte count. SIZEADD adds that count to TARGETSIZE; BUFFER contributes NUMV instead. The fixed header begins the count at fifteen bytes. An appended HALT contributes five, just as an explicit HALT does.

The count may not exceed ASM86's 8192-byte image limit. Every selected instruction form has a fixed encoding length; there is no immediate shortening or branch relaxation. The count therefore remains independent of forward-reference values.

The rejection source fits the text buffer but its buffer declarations exceed the machine-image bound. This distinguishes the image check from the existing text-byte check. A failure still occurs before output creation, so an older .ASM is not replaced.

title: Bounding generated source
description: Account for target definitions and completed assembly lines.
why: A translator should respect the assembler's source and name limits as well as its byte-image limit.
explain:
DEFS begins at one for I_ENTRY. NEWDEF counts each emitted user definition and refuses a count above 256. EMITCHAR now counts line feeds in OUTLINES and refuses more than 4000 assembly lines. The check happens before a successful output file is reported.

These are separate resources: a label emits no machine bytes, while a short DB row may emit many bytes on one line. Counting only output bytes would not protect the other limits. The generated template lines fit within ASM86's physical line width.

The name test uses the longest permitted IR spelling. U_ plus that name exactly fits the assembler's name bound. A longer name is rejected by NAMEARG before it can create invalid assembly. Duplicate and undefined user names are still diagnosed by ASM86, which owns address resolution.

title: An unconditional transfer
description: Use a near jump to a prefixed symbolic target.
why: JMP lets one basic block transfer to another without depending on a short displacement.
explain:
JMP name emits the near form JMP U_name. Its displacement is resolved by ASM86 from the following instruction to the named label. The target can be forward or backward within the program segment.

The table marks JMP as a terminal control boundary. FLOW requires the expression stack to be empty; LAST suppresses an unnecessary fall-through exit when JMP is the last statement. The translator does not prove that a jump targets code rather than data.

The test jumps over a nonzero EXIT to a zero EXIT. The generated name stays symbolic in the .ASM file, which demonstrates why the translator need not maintain a second address-resolution mechanism.

title: Testing the accumulator
description: Lower a conditional transfer through a nearby opposite branch.
why: A conditional transfer must reach any label in the bounded image, even though an 8088 conditional branch is short.
explain:
JZ compares AX with zero, branches around a near JMP when the condition is false, and otherwise takes that near JMP. JNZ uses the opposite short condition. AX is retained, the expression stack must be empty, and arithmetic flags are scratch.

A ? in the template inserts the current branch number as four decimal digits. FOUR preserves all word registers while sending those digits through EMITCHAR. BRANCHNO advances once per conditional statement, and every repeated ? in that pattern uses the same value. Labels I0001 and so forth are separate from all U_ names.

NEWDEF counts the generated skip label as well as user definitions. The only short displacement is across the near JMP itself, so a distant user target cannot overflow that short branch. The test takes its zero branch and avoids a nonzero exit.

title: Unsigned comparisons
description: Compare a saved left word with AX and branch on the result.
add: EQ NE ULT ULE UGT UGE
why: A comparison needs the same two-operand order as subtraction and a clear choice of signedness.
explain:
The comparison patterns pop the left word into BX, execute CMP BX,AX, then use an opposite short condition around a near JMP. EQ and NE compare equality; ULT, ULE, UGT, and UGE interpret both words as unsigned. AX retains the right operand rather than becoming a Boolean value.

Effect four consumes a saved word and then requires the expression stack to be empty. Thus a conditional edge and its fall-through edge agree on depth zero. A comparison cannot discard an unrelated saved expression value. BX and flags are scratch.

The test compares 65535 with one and takes the unsigned greater-than branch. A signed interpretation of those bits would produce a different result. Missing operands remain translation-time stack errors.

title: Signed comparisons
description: Interpret the same word bits as two's-complement values.
why: Signed ordering differs from unsigned ordering when the high bit is set. It must be requested explicitly.
explain:
SLT, SLE, SGT, and SGE use the 8086 signed comparison conditions after CMP BX,AX. Words with bit fifteen set represent -32768 through -1; other words represent zero through 32767. LIT still uses unsigned spelling, so 65535 supplies the bit pattern for -1.

The operand order, consumed stack word, generated skip name, and retained AX are the same as for unsigned comparisons. Equality needs no signed variant because equal bit patterns compare equal either way.

The test takes -1 less than one. It contrasts with the unsigned test while using the same numeric literal spellings. No signed arithmetic overflow exception is added: ordinary ADD and SUB still wrap as words.

title: Calling a procedure
description: Balance expression temporaries before native calls and returns.
why: A repeated computation can be placed under a label and called by name.
explain:
CALL emits a near CALL U_name and RET emits the matching near return. AX carries an input and a returned result by convention. Other ordinary registers and flags are scratch unless the procedure explicitly preserves them through its own program logic.

Both operations require expression depth zero. Native CALL puts a return offset on SS:SP; the called block may use balanced expression temporaries above that offset. The static empty-boundary rule prevents POP from treating the return address as an expression operand. There is no parameter list or automatic local-variable frame.

Place procedure bodies after a terminating main path or jump around them. A label alone does not prevent fall-through. Native call depth and recursion are not bounded by DEPTH; keep the reserved high stack area clear and call nesting modest. The test returns a zero result from ANSWER to the main EXIT.

title: Preparing DOS registers
description: Move words between AX and the three DOS argument registers.
add: TOBX TOCX TODX FROMBX FROMCX FROMDX
why: DOS handle services take arguments in BX, CX, and DX. Small register-transfer operations connect the accumulator model to that interface.
explain:
TOBX, TOCX, and TODX copy AX into the named register. FROMBX, FROMCX, and FROMDX copy it back into AX. Each lowers to one ordinary word MOV, changes no expression-stack depth, and leaves arithmetic flags unchanged.

These registers are not independent IR variables. Binary operators and pointer operations use BX as scratch. Prepare DOS argument registers after any computation which might disturb them, then load AX with the service number and call DOS. Values which must survive arbitrary procedures belong in named storage.

No segment register or SP transfer is provided. DS remains the program segment, pointers are offsets within it, and the expression/call-stack convention remains intact. The test saves zero in DX, disturbs AX, then retrieves the saved value for EXIT.

title: Calling DOS and testing carry
description: Use INT 21H with a checked, immediate carry branch.
why: A useful translation target must perform console and file I/O without an outside runtime library.
explain:
DOS emits INT 21H. AX supplies the service and, where required, an AL argument; BX, CX, and DX supply its other documented arguments. AX and other documented DOS results remain available afterward. DOS is an empty-expression-stack boundary.

JC and JNC use an opposite short carry condition around a near JMP. They must be the next nonempty statement after DOS. HASCARRY enforces that rule during translation: effect six establishes a pending carry result and effect seven consumes it; another instruction or label clears it. Comments and blank lines emit nothing and do not consume it.

The test deliberately tries to close the invalid handle FFFFH. DOS must set carry; JC selects the success path of this test. That path displays I with function 02H and returns zero through EXIT. A carry branch without a preceding DOS operation is a translation error. Check the DOS manual for each service's result registers and carry convention; the translator does not infer them.
